problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=3.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ find the principal axes of the curve.

examples.problem: Consider the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/4114e6536f57106949ed39a6ae4979646a0dd58c5690d7e7bcf9ffed15de8086.png) and the quadratic curve $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=1,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
examples.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/771d020606de64641ab305039a0c9a9de926080e83707b270a333b5775a8e028.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/54a77383e863630dfd4e21a796801001aaed3084f1097bca62ef4a098e20b405.png)

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/e0d71ad9216b9fa7c1831e6874b9a97bba9c1d9c5dbd6d9664635ed468d82a4c.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/83fd398b476c1c749346754a05c7f4071a98ab61453405a99ad8fcff65e38aaf.png)

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\qquad$ ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/8f0d84bb5c3ae37714c781b5dafbba1ae7de8561234ca558d3da2dcbfa9d75cf.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/293ad98697d595e3e0049aae93e54209b6d17aa92eb131b57791f211167690fc.png)

feedback.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $2{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+10{x}_{2}^{2}=44?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+10{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-12\lambda +11 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =11,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $11{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}11{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} & =44 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{44} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{11})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $2$ and $2\sqrt{11}.$
